text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game: each private token gives me 1 point but costs 0.75 to each other member, while group account tokens return 0.75 to everyone. I'm trying to set up the formula for my total points based on how many tokens I keep private versus contribute.

Keeping tokens private is individually dominant since 1 > 0.75, even though it's socially wasteful (private gives net -1.25 total versus group's +0.75) -- a classic free-rider dilemma. If everyone keeps everything private, each member ends up with 20 points total.

Since this is a 10-round repeated game, cooperation could pay off better long-term -- if everyone contributed fully to group, each would net 60 instead of 20. I'm leaning toward opening cooperatively by contributing all 20 tokens to the group as a signal, while staying ready to adjust if others defect.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: each token kept privately is worth 1 point to me but costs each other member 0.75 points, so my total depends on my own kept tokens plus the externalities from everyone else's private holdings.

Simplifying with contributions g_i to the group fund, my payoff reduces to a baseline plus a small penalty for my own kept tokens and a larger bonus from others' group contributions—meaning keeping tokens is personally cheap but socially costly, while contributing to the group is personally modest but benefits everyone collectively.

Checking the math: an individual token kept yields me +1 directly but costs others 0.75 each, a net social loss, whereas a token put in the group yields only 0.75 total but spread with no loss. So the social optimum is everyone contributing all 20 tokens, which would net each person 105 points, yet since others' contributions don't depend on my choice, keeping tokens is still individually dominant despite being collectively worse — the classic public goods dilemma.

Given this is a repeated 10-round game, I think opening with a generous contribution makes sense to signal cooperative intent and see how the group responds, so I'll start by giving the full 20 tokens in round one and adjust from there based on others' behavior.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure of this public goods game—keeping a token private gives me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75, while putting it in the group account only nets me 0.75 with no effect on others, so I'm trying to figure out the actual incentive comparison here.

Individually, keeping private dominates since 1 > 0.75, making group contribution a dominated strategy for me alone. But I'm realizing full defection by everyone leads to a terrible collective outcome since each person absorbs -0.75 from the other three keeping their tokens too, so I'm recalculating what happens if everyone keeps everything versus everyone contributing fully to see which scenario actually leaves people better off.

Full cooperation gives each 15 more, so the Nash equilibrium of zero contributions is worse for everyone collectively even though keeping tokens private is individually dominant. Since contributing hurts my own payoff slightly but helps the group substantially, I think it's reasonable to try cooperating first, perhaps contributing all 20 as an opening move.

Computing the extremes: if everyone keeps everything, each ends with 20 points per round versus 60 if everyone fully cooperates—cooperation is clearly better collectively even though defection is individually dominant each round. Given it's a 10-round repeated game, I'll lean toward starting cooperative by contributing fully in round one to signal good faith and see how others respond before deciding my strategy for later rounds.
